title: AQA Power and Conflict Poetry: Comparison Guide, Theme Map & Exam Strategy
description: AQA Power and Conflict GCSE guide covering the 15-poem anthology, theme mapping, comparison choices, integrated essay structure and a practical revision strategy.

children: The Power and Conflict anthology is easier to revise when the 15 poems are treated as a comparison network rather than 15 separate essays. In AQA English Literature Paper 2, students are given one named anthology poem and compare it with another poem from the same cluster.
What the comparison is testing

Knowledge matters because the second poem is not printed, but marks come from using that knowledge to compare ideas, methods and perspectives. A strong response keeps both poems in the same argument rather than writing two separate mini-essays.
Build a theme map
Human and political power: Ozymandias, London, My Last Duchess and Checking Out Me History can create useful links.
Power of nature: The Prelude, Storm on the Island, Exposure and Ozymandias can be useful.
War and immediate conflict: The Charge of the Light Brigade, Bayonet Charge and Exposure offer contrasting perspectives.
Memory, trauma and aftermath: Remains, War Photographer, Poppies, Kamikaze and The Emigrée provide useful connections.
Identity, belonging and control: Checking Out Me History, The Emigrée, Kamikaze and Tissue can be compared through different forms of power.
Do not memorise one fixed pairing

A pairing is useful only if it answers the question actually set. Revise two or three possible connections for the poems you know best and practise deciding which pairing creates the clearest argument for a particular theme.
Integrated comparison paragraph
Open with an idea about both poems, not the name of poem one.
Use evidence from the printed poem and analyse a method.
Bring in the second poem to extend, challenge or complicate the same idea.
Compare choices such as voice, imagery, form, structure, rhythm, perspective or tone.
Explain what the similarity or difference reveals about the theme.
Form and structure are often underused

Poetry gives students methods beyond individual words: stanza pattern, rhyme, rhythm, enjambment, caesura, shifts in speaker, cyclical structures, narrative perspective and changes in tone. Terminology is useful only when it helps explain meaning.
Context should stay attached to interpretation

Biographical or historical context can be useful, but it should not become a detached paragraph. Ask whether it helps explain the poet's viewpoint, form, image or relationship between individual experience and wider conflict.
Practical revision system
Maintain basic knowledge of all 15 poems while developing deeper control of a smaller flexible set.
Create a theme grid with at least two possible comparison choices for each major idea.
Learn short, flexible evidence from your strongest poems.
Practise two-minute pairing decisions from random question themes.
Write integrated comparison paragraphs before full timed essays.
Common comparison mistakes
Writing all of poem A and then all of poem B.
Choosing a familiar second poem when the thematic connection is weak.
Comparing only subject matter and not methods.
Forcing context into every paragraph.
Memorising a model essay so rigidly that it does not answer the actual question.
